name: Beach
notes: Sandy beaches above the tide line: salt- and sand-tolerant pioneers (creeping vines, succulent herbs, sea rocket) with coconut, screw pine and sea grape on tropical strands and sea buckthorn/pine on temperate ones. Drawn on Indo-Pacific and Caribbean strands, Atlantic Europe and eastern North America.

canopy.name: Coconut palm

growth.juvenile_note: The husked nut lies on the sand and after 2-6 months a pointed shoot pushes out of one end while the nut's flesh feeds the seedling. First leaves are entire, stiff, strap-like blades split only at the tip (bifid), in a stemless fan-like rosette; pinnate fronds come later, and a trunk rises after ~3-5 years, widening from a bulbous base ('bole').
growth.source: Wikipedia Coconut (tall palms bear at 6-10 yr, live 60-100 yr; ~11 months from female flower opening to harvest; up to 15 inflorescences/yr; ~80 nuts/yr, up to 150; nut ~1.4 kg; largely cross-pollinated, dwarfs selfing); ICRAF Agroforestree (tall selections 24-30 m, flowers after ~6th yr); germination from FAO coconut guides

canopy.source: Palm of tropical coasts worldwide; height 15-30 m. Leaning trunk, feather crown; sea-dispersed nuts. Standard floras and Kew POWO for the name.

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling sprouts from a woody, wedge-shaped key as a stemless rosette of long, stiff, strap-like leaves with small prickles on margins and keel, spiralling in three ranks. After a couple of years a trunk appears, soon propped on thick aerial stilt roots; it stays a single leafy tuft on a stem until it starts to flower and branch.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (male trees flower every 2 months, females 1-3 times a year; small insects such as bees and wind pollinate; head 4-20 cm wide, 8-30 cm long; keys yellow, orange or red with a green top; 1-2 years from pollination to ripe fruit); crop and decay estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling on the upper beach; its first leaves are already the typical almost circular, thick, leathery blades with red veins, often larger on saplings than on the adult. On windy dunes it sprawls into a low, many-stemmed shrub; in shelter it becomes a short, crooked tree.
growth.source: Wikipedia Coccoloba uvifera (whitish-green flowers on long spikes, cross-pollination by insects incl. honey bees, fruit ~2 cm green to purplish-red in grape-like bunches, eaten raw or as jelly and wine; salt tolerant, moderately tolerant of shade and drought, no frost); growth and ages estimated from Florida extension notes

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates by a remote tube; the first leaves are narrow and grass-like (undivided eophylls), each later leaf adds folds until costapalmate fans appear. For 10-30 years (up to 60 under forest) it is a stemless clump of fans while the stem grows DOWN then up (saxophone shape); then a trunk rises clad in criss-cross split leaf bases (boots).
growth.source: USDA Silvics of N America (Brown; 9 m in 16 yr cultivated, shade tolerant); Palmpedia (germination from 18 days; 15-30 yr to a visible trunk in nature); Plant Real Florida (10-15+ yr to trunk, ~15 cm trunk/yr, 9-12 m palms 70-95 yr); UT Austin palm pages (saxophone growth); first seed and lifespan estimated

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers 6 mm, creamy white, Apr-Aug in S Florida, 4-6 weeks from mid-July in N Carolina; bee-pollinated; black drupe-like berries 5-13 mm ripen in fall; ~1.5 million ripe fruits/ha/yr); Palmpedia (fruit ripens in winter); thin sweet flesh eaten raw

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two small oval cotyledons, then narrow willow-like leaves, grey-green above and silvery-scaled beneath, on a thin single stem. For its first years the plant is a wispy, spiny sprig; soon it throws up root suckers all around, so a young plant becomes a spreading, silvery, thorny thicket rather than a single bush.
growth.source: USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual (Hippophae: flowers Mar-Apr before leaves, fruit Sep-Oct persisting to March, epigeal, 40-day germination tests); ICRAF Agroforestree (fruits from ~3 yr, peak 7-8 yr, 10-20 cm/yr, dies under >50% canopy); Wikipedia (4-5 yr from seed to fruit, productive ~30 yr). Max lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (dioecious, wind-pollinated, tiny yellow flowers before leaves, drupe 5-12 mm reddish-orange ripening late Jul-early Oct, 5-7 kg per plant); USDA WPSM (fruits persist to March); Wikipedia (berries 6-8 mm, 270-480 mg, edible, sour). Fruit set estimated.

shrub.name: Bay cedar

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling comes up on the beach crest from a floated, hard-coated nutlet: a short woody stem with narrow, fleshy, grey-hairy leaves crowded at its tip. It branches low and irregularly, so a few years on it is a stiff, twisted, grey-green knot of a shrub, the leaves always in tufts at the ends of the twigs.
growth.source: Wunderlin & Hansen, Atlas of Florida Plants and Little 1979 (Suriana maritima: shrub 1-3 m, rarely a small tree to 6 m, on beach ridges and coastal rock); germination, growth rate, first flowering and lifespan estimated

shrub.source: Suriana maritima, bay cedar: pantropical on sandy beach ridges and rocky seashores just above the tide (Florida, Caribbean, Pacific and Indian Ocean strands), grey-hairy shrub 1-3 m (rarely 6 m) with narrow spatulate leaves crowded at the twig tips and yellow five-petalled flowers; the nutlets float — Kew POWO; Wunderlin & Hansen, Atlas of Florida Plants; Whistler 1992 Flowers of the Pacific Island Seashore.

shrub.name: Coast saltbush

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings appear on the drift line and the seaward face of the foredune: a small upright shoot with opposite, then alternate, silvery-scurfy oblong leaves. It thickens fast into a low, spreading, silver-grey bush of brittle woody stems that traps blown sand and wrack around its base.
growth.source: VicFlora and Flora of Australia (Atriplex cinerea: dioecious shrub to 1-2.5 m on beaches and foredunes, leaves 2-6 cm, flowering spring-summer); germination, growth rate and lifespan estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings come up in spring on bare foredune sand as a single narrow grass shoot with thin, rolled leaves and deep roots. By the end of the first season it is a small tuft; in the second it tillers heavily and sends rhizomes 0.6-1.8 m a year, new shoots pushing up through blown sand. The tall arching culms with flat golden spikelets come later.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Uniola paniculata): 30 days cold-moist at 4 C then 78-89% germination at alternating temperatures; seedlings establish in the first season and tiller extensively by the second; lateral spread 0.6-1.8 m a year; sand burial stimulates growth; flowers Jun-Nov; about 30% of ovaries set seed. Wikipedia: 1-2 m. First flowering and clump lifespan estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: a hair-thin shoot with wiry, inrolled leaves, emerging in May; it tillers and sends thin rhizomes into a small dense tuft, with no flowers in year one and only a few in year two. Mature stands are a dense turf of fine, wiry stems that lodge into swirled 'cowlicks'.

ground.name: Seashore dropseed

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are scarce; most new plants are shoots from long, scaly, creeping rhizomes running under the sand. Each shoot is a short stiff culm with small leaves set in two neat ranks, their blades rolled tight and sharp-tipped, so a patch reads as a low, wiry, grey-green turf that thickens as sand blows over it.
growth.source: Flora of North America vol. 25 (Sporobolus virginicus: rhizomatous perennial, culms 10-50(70) cm, leaves distichous, involute); Whistler 1992 (Pacific strand); seedling and lifespan estimated

ground.source: Sporobolus virginicus, seashore dropseed: pantropical and warm-temperate on sandy beaches, foredunes and salt-marsh edges (SE US, Caribbean, Indo-Pacific, Australia), rhizomatous, culms 10-50 (to 70) cm with two-ranked stiff rolled leaves and dense narrow pale panicles; a regular of the Pes-caprae strand — Kew POWO; Flora of North America vol. 25; Whistler 1992 Flowers of the Pacific Island Seashore.

ground.name: Dune brittlestem
ground.origin: European and N American coastal dunes

repro.note: The mycelium lives in the sand on the dead, buried roots and rhizomes of marram and lyme grass; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading along the buried grass; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Psathyrella ammophila, dune brittlestem: saprotroph on the buried dead roots of marram (Ammophila) on mobile and embryo dunes and the upper beach of Atlantic and North Sea coasts, also on North American Ammophila dunes; cap 1.5-4 cm date-brown drying tan, stem rooted deep in the sand — Index Fungorum; Phillips 2006 Mushrooms; Kits van Waveren 1985 (Psathyrella monograph).

cap.form: convex then flattened cap 1.5-4 cm, date-brown drying pale tan from the centre
cap.notes: often half-buried, sand clinging to the cap

underside.type: gills pale brown turning dark purple-brown

appearance.habit: single or a few among marram on loose dune sand
appearance.seasonal: fruits in autumn after rain, then rots in days
appearance.silhouette: small brown caps poking out of bare sand by marram
appearance.refs: Index Fungorum; Phillips 2006; First Nature (Psathyrella ammophila)

ground.name: Dune puffball
ground.origin: Europe and North America, sandy ground

repro.note: The mycelium lives in open, dry sand; the ball forms buried, breaks loose and lies on the surface for months, puffing spores from its top pore when wind or rain strikes it. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium in the sand; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Disciseda candida: small puffball of open dry sandy ground, fixed dunes and sandy grassland in Europe and North America; ball 1-3 cm, forming half-buried, its lower half crusted with sand, then breaking free and lying upside down with a pore on top — Index Fungorum; Pegler, Laessoe & Spooner 1995 British Puffballs, Earthstars and Stinkhorns.

cap.notes: white to buff, ageing grey-brown; spore mass olive-brown

appearance.seasonal: forms in autumn; the dry balls persist into spring
